newsitem.title: GREECE: Greece says could begin direct talks with Turkey.
newsitem.headline: Greece says could begin direct talks with Turkey.

text.p: Feuding NATO members Greece and Turkey could begin direct talks to resolve their long-festering disputes, Greek Foreign Minister Theodoros Pangalos told an Athens newspaper on Monday.

A watershed agreement at the NATO summit in Madrid this month had lifted the threat of war and made it possible for the Aegean Sea neighbours to talk face to face without third-party mediation, Pangalos told the major daily Ta Nea.
Athens had in the past turned down repeated calls from Ankara to begin dialogue on all contentious issues, saying this would mean it was prepared to negotiate its sovereignty.
Greece had insisted that Ankara should lift its threats of war and take its territorial claims against Greece to the International Court of Justice at The Hague before direct talks could begin.
"Within this (Madrid) framework Greece can now talk to Turkey directly," Pangalos was quoted as saying. "And this is a major political development."
The U.S.-brokered "convergence of views" signed in Madrid on July 8 committed Greece and Turkey to respect each other's rights and renounce use of force.
Eighteen months ago the two NATO members were on the brink of war over a deserted Aegean islet known as Imia in Greek and Kardak in Turkish. A clash was averted after last-minute U.S. intervention.

The Madrid agreement avoids mention of specific problems, such as territorial waters in the Aegean, minority rights in both countries, and the divided island of Cyprus. But it signals the will to end years of vicious bickering.
Pangalos said the mediation of third parties such as the United States or the European Union would no longer be necessary to discuss issues that affected the two countries.
"As grown-up representatives of grown-up countries it is possible now to meet and discuss all issues that affect the two countries," Pangalos said.
Pangalos said political instability in Turkey was holding it back and it had to choose between the Moslem world and western European-style democracy.
"Turkey cannot remain with one foot in Islam and one in Europe," he was quoted as saying.
Turkey's Islamist prime minister, Necmettin Erbakan, resigned last month under pressure from the secularist army and was replaced by Mesut Yilmaz.
